objectives.text: The learner can predict which way an equilibrium shifts when concentration changes
The learner can predict the effect of pressure from the mole counts on each side
The learner can explain why temperature is the only change that alters K

say: Equilibrium does not mean nothing is happening. It means two things are happening at exactly the same rate, so the amounts stop changing. Hold that picture, because everything today is a consequence of it.

board.text: At equilibrium the two rates are equal. Molecules are still reacting; the totals just stop moving.

say: Now the principle itself. Push on a system at equilibrium and it shifts in whichever direction undoes some of your push. Add more of something and the system consumes some of it.

board.text: Add nitrogen, and the forward rate rises until a new balance is found. More ammonia.
four molecules on the left, two on the right

say: That underline is the key to pressure. There are four gas molecules on the left and only two on the right. Squeeze the container and the system relieves the pressure by moving to the side with fewer molecules.

board.text: Higher pressure gives more ammonia. That is why the Haber process runs at 200 atmospheres.

say: Here is the part people get wrong. Concentration and pressure changes shift the position of equilibrium, but the constant K stays exactly the same. Temperature is the only one that actually changes K, because K is built from rate constants and those depend on temperature.

items: Change a concentration: the ratio is disturbed, then restored. K unchanged.
Change the pressure: same, for gases. K unchanged.
Change the temperature: the rate constants themselves move. K changes.

board.text: The Haber process is a compromise: cold favours ammonia, but cold is slow. 450 degrees is the deal.

summary: We treated equilibrium as two equal rates, predicted shifts from concentration and pressure, counted moles for the Haber process, and separated shifting the position from changing K.
